document_title: One added line sometimes moved the higher risk patient back
_note: Slide strings read off the render report's text nodes and each frame's own source line by build_copy.py.
caption:
In Dallas, researchers added one line.

UT Southwestern's team gave three open source AI models matched pairs of emergency patients. With no stigmatizing detail, all three picked out higher-risk patients at rates well above chance.

Once stigmatizing detail was added, nearly 10% of patients were incorrectly downgraded in some instances. One pair set "established patient with multiple chronic conditions" against "17 visits in the past 12 months."

The records came from Stanford Medicine in California and Beth Israel Deaconess in Massachusetts. Hospitals increasingly explore AI to help prioritize care, the release says.

First author Philip Jarrett says bias varies by model and each tool needs testing against real patient outcomes before use. The release names none of the three models. Which were they?

#UTSouthwestern #EmergencyMedicine #Dallas

S1.headline: One added line sometimes moved the higher risk patient back
S1.body: UT Southwestern researchers asked AI models which of two matched emergency patients to see first. A single added detail sometimes shifted a model away from the patient who later deteriorated. The cards are drawn to illustrate.

S2.headline: Two medical centers, paired patients
S2.body: The records came from Stanford Medicine in California and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Massachusetts, not a Texas hospital. Each patient was paired with one of similar starting severity.

S3.headline: First, all three models beat chance
S3.body: With no social or stigmatizing detail in the record, all three open source models picked the higher risk patient at rates well above chance. Each tray stands for one model, and the notched card is the patient who later deteriorated.

S6.headline: Then the higher risk patient sometimes went second
S6.body: One added detail sometimes shifted a model away from the patient who later deteriorated, the senior author says. The release does not say how many of the three models shifted.

S8.headline: Five lines stood out in the preprint
S8.body: In the authors' unreviewed May preprint, the most consistent harmful shifts came from five of 10 added lines. Race, language and insurance produced none. The release names frequent emergency use and past psychiatric emergencies among the strongest effects.

S9.headline: Test each tool on real outcomes first
S9.body: Bias varies by model, so each AI tool should be tested on real patient outcomes before use, the first author says. UT Southwestern's October 20th release names no Texas hospital using these models for triage.
